title: An Atlas Document's category is encoded in its identifier, so its mutability is machine-inferable
content:
A.1.2.2.1 states that the four document categories have "unique and non-overlapping rules for validity of their Document Identifiers," so "the category of an Atlas Document can be inferred from its Document Identifier." The specific partitions are:

- **Immutable** (A.1.2.2.1.1): at most three layers deep.
- **Primary** (A.1.2.2.1.2): four layers or deeper, and cannot contain zeros.
- **Supporting** (A.1.2.2.1.3): always contains at least one zero.
- **Accessory** (A.1.2.2.1.4): always contains letters beyond the leading 'A'.

This is a deliberate collapse of two things most systems keep separate: an item's *address* and its *governance class*. Because depth determines category and category determines how a document may be modified, position in the tree **is** the mutability rule. You cannot move a document without changing what may be done to it, and you cannot smuggle a permanent principle into an easily-amended slot or vice versa.

The non-overlap requirement is what makes it a real constraint rather than a naming convention — every valid identifier belongs to exactly one category, so there is no ambiguous middle where a document's amendability could be argued. The trade-off is rigidity: reorganizing the tree is not a cosmetic refactor, it is a governance act, and A.1.2.1.1.1 concedes that in early iterations formal identifiers will not yet be implemented for all Document Types.
description: Immutable ≤3 layers deep; Primary ≥4 layers with no zeros; Supporting contains at least one zero; Accessory contains letters. Non-overlapping rules make category derivable from the ID alone.
